artwork.title: La Belle Ferronnière
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Wilfredor, 2024, via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

lessons.title: A name that is not hers

n1.text: A young woman in red, seen to the waist behind a stone ledge, against a black background. Leonardo painted her in Milan in the 1490s.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: Come close and take your time. A portrait is a meeting, and she will not hurry.

q1.text: In Milan then, how were most portraits posed?

b1a.text: Yes. Milan's elite liked strict profiles. Leonardo turned this sitter three-quarters instead: her body one way, her head back the other.

b1b.text: That was Leonardo's change, not the custom.

correction.truth: Milanese portraits were mostly in strict profile. Leonardo broke the habit with a three-quarter turn.
The Milanese custom was strict profile, like a head on a coin. Leonardo chose a three-quarter turn.

n2.text: Leonardo wrote it down as a rule for painters: never turn the head the same way as the body. Here her shoulders angle one way and her face turns back.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: Turn the body one way and the head the other. A figure that turns has somewhere to look.

q2.text: Where does her famous name, La Belle Ferronnière, come from?

correction.truth: It comes from a French legend about an ironmonger's wife who became a mistress of King Francis I.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; the Barber Institute, Birmingham.

correction.truth: The name comes from a later French legend. The Louvre's own title says it is wrong.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; the Barber Institute, Birmingham.

b2c.text: Yes. Legend told of an ironmonger's wife who became a mistress of King Francis I. The Louvre's title calls the name wrong: "dit à tort".

n3.text: So who was she really? Scholars disagree. The names proposed most often are Lucrezia Crivelli, Beatrice d'Este and Isabella of Aragon, all from the court of Milan.

voice.speaker: leonardo
voice.text: You want a name. Look at her instead: the face, the gaze, the turn. That is what I painted.

q3.text: Has anyone proven who sat for this portrait?

b3a.text: She is the favourite, not a proven answer.

correction.tempting: A poem of the time praises a portrait of a Lucrezia by Leonardo.
correction.truth: The poem does not describe this panel. Many scholars favour Lucrezia, but nothing proves it.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; Galerie magazine (2026); the poems in Richter's edition (1883).

b3b.text: Yes. Many favour Lucrezia Crivelli because of a poem praising a Leonardo portrait of a Lucrezia; others prefer Beatrice or Isabella. Nothing settles it.

correction.tempting: The National Gallery in London suggested her in 2011.
correction.truth: Others prefer Lucrezia or Isabella. No identification has been proven.
correction.evidence: The National Art Center, Tokyo (2026); Galerie magazine (2026).

n4.text: Now her clothes: a thin band across her forehead, hair gathered behind, a square neckline, sleeves tied on with ribbons.

q4.text: What can her clothes tell us?

b4a.text: Clothes date her; they cannot name her.

correction.tempting: The jewel on her forehead looks personal.
correction.truth: Other women at the court wore the same fashion, Beatrice d'Este among them.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery, London; the National Art Center, Tokyo.

b4b.text: Yes. Her band, hairstyle, neckline and ribboned sleeves were the fashion of north Italian courts in the 1490s.

correction.truth: Her dress and hair follow north Italian court fashion of the 1490s.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery, London; the National Art Center, Tokyo.

n5.text: From the French royal collection she passed to the Louvre in 1793. In 2026 she travelled to Tokyo, her first time in Japan. Her real name is still unknown.

lessons.takeaway: Leonardo painted this young woman in Milan in the 1490s, turning her head against her body; her famous name comes from a French legend, and nobody has proven who she was.
